plan.angle: Keep everything except chapter 4. Replace 'the new grocery-purchase study (DOM, Oct 29, 2026)' with: 'What happens to what people buy? A Danish study of supermarket receipts (JAMA Network Open, 2026)'. Give 293 GLP-1 starters versus 884 matched non-users, and call it observational purchase data, not what people actually ate. Say the changes were 'modest' and 'linked to' starting the drug. Say which GLP-1 medicines it covered only as the paper reports them, and don't say tirzepatide unless the paper does. Use the DOM Oct 29 paper only if a human or the scriptwriter opens its abstract and confirms the drugs, population, design and findings. Otherwise drop it. Main human anchor: Heise 2023 Diabetes Care (type 2 diabetes, tirzepatide vs semaglutide vs placebo, appetite and energy intake at a test lunch). Label every brain-reward finding by species. Chapter 5: SURMOUNT-4 shows weight regain after switching to placebo, not food noise directly. Say 'many people report hunger coming back' only as an unsourced, plainly hedged observation, or leave it out.

plan.why: Next topic in the Lane A queue. Lane A is the engine (median about 232 min, about 6.6× other GLP-1 long-forms), and this one sits next to What to Eat and Side Effects for suggested traffic. The body rests on settled mechanism and trial evidence. | fact-check: The Lane A topic, safety framing, chapter plan and title are sound. The title is 45 characters and its first sentence answers it. Mechanism plus human-study chapters can be fully sourced. One problem: I could not confirm that the 'new grocery-purchase study (Diabetes Obes Metab, Oct 29, 2026)' exists. Several extended searches found only one supermarket-receipt study. It is Danish and appeared in JAMA Network Open in early 2026: 'Consumer Food Purchases After Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonist Initiation', from the SMIL cohort at Steno Diabetes Center Copenhagen. It followed 1,177 adults: 293 who started a GLP-1 receptor agonist and 884 matched non-users. It found modest drops in calories, sugar, carbohydrate and saturated fat per 100 g of food bought, a slight rise in protein and a shift toward less ultra-processed food. I also saw a DOM record (dom.71408) but couldn't open it (403), so I can't say what it reports. Verified human appetite anchor for tirzepatide: Heise et al., Diabetes Care 2023;46(5):998–1004. This randomized, double-blind trial in people with type 2 diabetes compared tirzepatide with semaglutide and placebo. Both drugs reduced appetite compared with placebo, and tirzepatide reduced energy intake at an all-you-can-eat lunch. Say 'people with type 2 diabetes' and don't give dose numbers on screen or in the narration. Label any semaglutide-only data as semaglutide. Most reward-system evidence ('wanting' vs 'liking') comes from rodents, so label it 'in mice/rats'. Don't claim tirzepatide's GIP part acts in the human brain; that's unproven in people. 'Food noise' is a lay term, not a diagnosis; keep it that way. Stopping chapter: SURMOUNT-4 measured weight regain, not food noise. Don't say it showed food noise returning; say only that weight was regained on placebo (+14.0% from week 36 to week 88), plus the don't-stop line.

package.description:
Tirzepatide and food noise: why it can go quiet, and what helps if it comes back.

Quick answer: in a 2023 randomized trial in adults with type 2 diabetes, people on tirzepatide rated their appetite lower and ate about 310 fewer calories at an all-you-can-eat lunch than the placebo group. The GIP brain role is mostly animal data. Nausea or constipation can make eating hard; raise it with your prescriber.

Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether tirzepatide is right for you, and don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own.

Sources:
Heise 2023, Diabetes Care: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36857477/
Sørensen 2026, JAMA Netw Open: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41587033/
Aronne 2024, JAMA (SURMOUNT-4): https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38078870/
Hayashi 2023, Nutrients: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38004203/

script.hook_pattern: Visceral 'you' scenario (10 p.m., not thinking about the cupboard), answered within 15 seconds, then an open loop (Danish supermarket receipts + what to do if the noise comes back) paid off in chapters 5–8

scenes.narration: It's ten at night. You're not hungry, and for once, you're not thinking about the snacks in the cupboard.

visual.stock_query: calm woman on sofa at night, relieved

scenes.narration: If you're on tirzepatide, here's the short answer to why. It copies two gut hormones, GLP-1 and GIP, and the leading explanation is that those signals turn down appetite through the brain.

visual.stock_query: gut sending glowing signals to brain

scenes.narration: In a randomized trial, people with type 2 diabetes on tirzepatide rated their appetite lower than on placebo, and at an all-you-can-eat lunch they ate about three hundred and ten fewer calories than the placebo group.

visual.stat_label: Less eaten at lunch vs placebo: tirzepatide 15 mg, type 2 diabetes, 28 weeks

scenes.narration: But that's only half the story. By the end, you'll know what Danish supermarket receipts revealed, and what to do if the noise ever turns back up.

visual.stock_query: curious shopping receipt with question mark

scenes.retention_device: Main open loop planted (pays off in chapters 5–8)

scenes.narration: We'll cover what food noise actually is, how the signal reaches your brain, which findings come from mice and which from people, and the habits with real evidence behind them.

items: How the signal reaches the brain

scenes.narration: Picture someone we'll call Dana. She's hypothetical, fifty-two, and for years food has been the loudest voice in her head.

visual.stock_query: thoughtful woman fifty with thought bubbles of food

scenes.narration: Three months into treatment, the volume has dropped. She's relieved, and a little worried. Is this quiet real? And will it last?
scenes.on_screen_text: Is it real? Will it last?

visual.stock_query: hopeful woman at kitchen table, slight worry

scenes.retention_device: Two questions to be answered in the payoff

scenes.narration: Quick note: this is general education. Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether tirzepatide is right for you.
scenes.retention_device: Trust signal before the deep dive

scenes.narration: So first, what is food noise? It isn't a medical diagnosis. It's an everyday phrase for persistent, intrusive thoughts about food.

visual.stock_query: head full of buzzing food thoughts

scenes.narration: Like planning your next snack while you're still eating lunch, or hearing the biscuit tin call from the other room.

visual.stock_query: biscuit tin calling from another room

scenes.narration: In twenty twenty-three, researchers in the journal Nutrients proposed a model for it. They linked food noise to food cue reactivity: your brain reacting strongly to the sight, smell or even the thought of food.

visual.stock_query: brain lighting up at smell of pizza

scenes.retention_device: Named concept, used again in habits chapter

scenes.narration: If you've felt like that's a willpower problem, you're not alone. And the biology says it isn't only that.

visual.myth: Food noise is just weak willpower
visual.fact: Appetite biology plays a real part
visual.stock_query: relieved person, weight lifted off shoulders

scenes.narration: Appetite is shaped by gut hormones, brain circuits and the food cues around you, all at the same time.
scenes.retention_device: Simple model to hang the rest on

scenes.narration: So where does a once-weekly medicine plug into all of that? It starts in your gut.

scenes.section: How does tirzepatide reach the brain?
scenes.narration: How does tirzepatide reach the brain? When you eat, your gut releases GLP-1 and GIP. Both help your pancreas release insulin when blood sugar rises.
scenes.on_screen_text: How does it reach the brain?

scenes.section: How does tirzepatide reach the brain?
scenes.narration: The prescribing label describes tirzepatide as acting on both the GIP and GLP-1 receptors, and links its weight loss to eating fewer calories, likely through effects on appetite.

scenes.section: How does tirzepatide reach the brain?
scenes.narration: Its half-life is about five days, which is why it's taken once a week and the signal stays switched on.

visual.stock_query: glowing signal light staying on all week

scenes.section: How does tirzepatide reach the brain?
scenes.narration: But here's where it gets interesting. Most of your brain sits behind a protective barrier that keeps big molecules out. So how does the message get through?

scenes.section: How does tirzepatide reach the brain?
scenes.narration: In mice, researchers tagged semaglutide, a related GLP-1 drug, with a glowing marker, and watched where it went. Rat experiments backed up the picture.

visual.stock_query: cute lab mouse with glowing map

scenes.section: How does tirzepatide reach the brain?
scenes.narration: It reached spots at the brain's edges where the barrier is leakier, including parts of the hindbrain and the hypothalamus, the brain's appetite control centre.

visual.stock_query: glowing dots at edges of brain

scenes.section: How does tirzepatide reach the brain?
scenes.narration: From there, it activated wider networks linked to hunger and fullness. That's animal data, but it's a map for where to look in people.

visual.stock_query: brain network lighting up like city map

scenes.section: How does tirzepatide reach the brain?
scenes.narration: GIP is newer territory. In mice, cells carrying GIP receptors were found in the hypothalamus, and switching those cells on made the mice eat less.

scenes.section: How does tirzepatide reach the brain?
scenes.narration: Big caveat: whether tirzepatide's GIP signal acts in the human brain hasn't been shown. In people, that's still an open question.

visual.myth: GIP is proven to act in the human brain
visual.fact: Shown in mice; unproven in people

scenes.section: How does tirzepatide reach the brain?
scenes.narration: So for Dana, the honest answer so far: GLP-1's appetite effects are well studied. The GIP part is promising, but mostly based on animals.

scenes.section: How does tirzepatide reach the brain?
scenes.narration: But fullness is one thing. Food noise feels different, a pull toward food even when you're full. That's the reward system, and that's where it gets surprising.
Do GLP-1 drugs change cravings? Deep in the brain sits a reward circuit that runs partly on dopamine. It helps explain why a warm cookie can feel urgent when a plain apple doesn't.

visual.stock_query: warm cookie glowing next to plain apple

scenes.narration: In twenty twelve, Swedish researchers gave rats a GLP-1 drug called exendin four directly into two reward areas, the ventral tegmental area and the nucleus accumbens.
The rats worked less hard to earn sugar, and they ate less food overall. Rats aren't people, but it showed GLP-1 signals can reach reward circuits, not just fullness ones.
So does anything like that happen in humans? A Dutch team put it to the test.
Forty-eight adults lay in a brain scanner looking at pictures of food. Some were lean, some had obesity, and some had obesity plus type 2 diabetes.

visual.stock_query: person in scanner viewing burger pictures

scenes.narration: During a short infusion of exenatide, an older GLP-1 drug, brain responses to food pictures dropped in reward and appetite areas like the insula and amygdala, in the participants with obesity.

visual.stat_label: Exenatide brain scans, food pictures, humans

scenes.narration: That's a different drug, given once, in a lab. It's not tirzepatide. But it's direct human evidence that GLP-1 signalling can dial down the brain's reaction to food cues.

visual.stock_query: volume dial turning down in brain

scenes.narration: Now cravings themselves. In a twenty twenty-one trial, seventy-two adults with obesity took semaglutide or placebo for twenty weeks.

visual.stock_query: group of adults at study clinic

scenes.narration: At a buffet lunch, the semaglutide group ate about thirty-five percent less than the placebo group. They also reported fewer food cravings and better control over eating.

visual.stat_label: Semaglutide vs placebo lunch intake, obesity, 20 weeks

scenes.narration: Again, that's semaglutide, not tirzepatide. Which brings us to the study you probably came for.

What do tirzepatide trials show about appetite? In a twenty twenty-three trial in Diabetes Care, one hundred and seventeen adults with type 2 diabetes were randomly assigned to tirzepatide, semaglutide or placebo.

visual.stock_query: three groups sorted by random draw

scenes.narration: It was double-blind and lasted twenty-eight weeks. Researchers measured appetite with rating scales, then served an all-you-can-eat lunch and measured what people ate.
Both drugs lowered appetite compared with placebo.

visual.stock_query: two arrows pointing down on hunger meter

scenes.narration: At that lunch, people on tirzepatide ate about three hundred and ten fewer calories than the placebo group.

visual.stat_label: Less eaten at lunch vs placebo: tirzepatide 15 mg, type 2 diabetes, 28 weeks
visual.stock_query: lunch tray with food left over

scenes.narration: People on semaglutide also ate less than placebo. Tirzepatide's drop was about sixty-four calories bigger.

visual.stat_label: Extra drop, tirzepatide 15 mg vs semaglutide 1 mg: not statistically significant
visual.stock_query: two lunch trays side by side

scenes.narration: And the difference between the two drugs wasn't statistically significant. So this study doesn't show that one beats the other on appetite.

visual.myth: This trial proved one drug wins on appetite

scenes.narration: Three hundred and ten calories is roughly a generous snack, left on the plate at a single meal.

visual.stock_query: snack left on plate, calm person walking away

scenes.narration: Keep the scope in mind: a small trial, people with type 2 diabetes, appetite measured in a lab. It tells us about hunger and intake, not about food noise exactly as people describe it.
For Dana, it's reassuring. The quiet she feels lines up with what trials measured, and it isn't just her trying harder.
But one thing trials can't see is your shopping basket. If appetite changes, does what you buy change too?

scenes.section: Do GLP-1 users buy different food?
scenes.narration: Do GLP-1 users buy different food? A Danish study, published in JAMA Network Open in twenty twenty-six, looked at supermarket receipts.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter card, payoff of the hook loop

scenes.section: Do GLP-1 users buy different food?
scenes.narration: Researchers compared two hundred and ninety-three adults who started a GLP-1 receptor agonist medicine with eight hundred and eighty-four matched adults who didn't.

visual.stat_label: GLP-1 starters vs matched non-users, Denmark
visual.stock_query: two groups of shoppers side by side

scenes.section: Do GLP-1 users buy different food?
scenes.narration: After people started, the food they bought had modestly fewer calories, less sugar, less carbohydrate and less saturated fat per hundred grams.

scenes.section: Do GLP-1 users buy different food?
scenes.narration: Protein went up slightly, and purchases shifted a little away from ultra-processed food.
scenes.retention_device: Extra detail, sets up habits chapter

scenes.section: Do GLP-1 users buy different food?
scenes.narration: Two important limits. It's observational, so these modest changes are linked to starting the medicine, not proven to be caused by it.

visual.myth: The drug caused these purchase changes

scenes.section: Do GLP-1 users buy different food?
scenes.narration: And receipts show what people bought, not what they actually ate.

visual.stock_query: receipt next to empty dinner plate

scenes.section: Do GLP-1 users buy different food?
scenes.narration: The paper looks at GLP-1 receptor agonists as a group, so it can't tell us what tirzepatide does specifically.

visual.stock_query: group of medicine pens, no labels

scenes.section: Do GLP-1 users buy different food?
scenes.narration: Still, it's a real-world hint that a quieter appetite might reach the checkout too. Modest, not magic.

scenes.section: Do GLP-1 users buy different food?
scenes.narration: Now, the part Dana worries about most. What happens if the noise comes back?

visual.stock_query: Dana looking at quiet kitchen, thoughtful

scenes.section: What if food noise comes back?
scenes.narration: What if food noise comes back? Start with what we know about stopping. In the SURMOUNT-four trial, seven hundred and eighty-three adults began tirzepatide.
scenes.on_screen_text: What if food noise comes back?

scenes.section: What if food noise comes back?
scenes.narration: They had obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, and no diabetes. After thirty-six weeks on tirzepatide, six hundred and seventy were randomized.

scenes.section: What if food noise comes back?
scenes.narration: Three hundred and thirty-five stayed on tirzepatide. Three hundred and thirty-five were switched to placebo, without knowing which they got.

scenes.section: What if food noise comes back?
scenes.narration: From week thirty-six to week eighty-eight, the placebo group regained fourteen percent of body weight, on average.

scenes.section: What if food noise comes back?
scenes.narration: The group that stayed on tirzepatide kept losing. Five point five percent more, on average.

visual.stat_label: Further weight change staying on tirzepatide, weeks 36–88

scenes.section: What if food noise comes back?
scenes.narration: Notice what that measured: body weight. It didn't measure food noise.

visual.fact: It measured weight regain on placebo
visual.stock_query: scale next to crossed-out thought bubble

scenes.section: What if food noise comes back?
scenes.narration: Some people say their hunger seems to come back after stopping. That's a personal report, not something this trial tested.

scenes.section: What if food noise comes back?
scenes.narration: So the key rule: don't switch, stop or change your medicine on your own. Any change is a plan to make with your prescriber.

scenes.section: What if food noise comes back?
scenes.narration: And even while on treatment, some people notice food thoughts getting louder in stressful or short-sleep weeks. If that's you, it doesn't mean you failed.

visual.stock_query: tired person at desk, kind reassurance

scenes.section: What if food noise comes back?
scenes.narration: This is where habits come in, and a couple of them have surprisingly strong evidence.

scenes.section: What if food noise comes back?
scenes.narration: One note: if food thoughts feel tied to bingeing, restricting or distress, that's worth raising with your doctor. Support exists, and it isn't about trying harder.
Which habits quiet food noise? Habit one: protect your sleep. In a meta-analysis of sleep studies, short sleep led people to eat about three hundred and eighty-five extra calories a day.

visual.stat_label: Extra daily intake after short sleep, meta-analysis

scenes.narration: Tired brains seem to want more food. A steady bedtime is an appetite tool, not just a wellness cliché.
Habit two: lean toward less processed food. In a tightly controlled NIH study, twenty adults ate about five hundred more calories a day on an ultra-processed diet than on a minimally processed one.

visual.stat_label: Extra daily intake, ultra-processed vs minimally processed

scenes.narration: Both diets offered matched amounts of calories, sugar, fat and fibre, and people could eat as much as they liked. The main difference was the processing.

visual.stock_query: two matched meal trays side by side

scenes.narration: Remember those Danish receipts? Shopping and appetite may be working on the same problem.
Habit three: slow down. A review of lab studies found that eating more slowly tended to mean eating less.
Try putting your fork down between bites, so fullness has time to catch up.
Habit four, and this one's our own tip: build meals around protein and fibre-rich plants, so they feel satisfying.
Habit five: change the cues. Food noise is tied to cue reactivity, remember? So move tempting snacks out of sight, and keep easy, filling options at eye level.
Habit six: notice the pattern without judging it. When does the noise get loud? Tired, stressed, skipped lunch? Patterns are information, not failure.
Habit seven: talk to your prescriber. If food noise comes back strongly, or common side effects like nausea or constipation make eating hard, that's worth a conversation.

So, back to Dana's questions. Is the quiet real? The evidence points that way: in a randomized trial in people with type 2 diabetes, tirzepatide reduced appetite and food intake compared with placebo.
Will it last? SURMOUNT-four measured weight, not food noise. People who stayed on tirzepatide kept losing weight, and people switched to placebo regained weight.
So if she and her prescriber ever plan a change, the habits she builds now are part of that plan.
scenes.on_screen_text: Habits are part of the plan

visual.stock_query: Dana and prescriber with plan sheet

scenes.narration: And if the noise turns up on a bad week, it's not a moral failing. It's biology she understands, with tools she can use.
Here's your food noise checklist. Protect your sleep. Choose less processed food. Eat slowly. Build meals around protein and fibre. Move food cues out of sight.
Notice your loud moments without judgement. And bring any changes to your prescriber, never adjust your medicine on your own.

factcheck.summary:
PASS, with 4 minor wording fixes. I checked every key number against its primary source and they are all accurate:
- **Tirzepatide appetite trial (Heise 2023, Diabetes Care):** double-blind, 117 adults with type 2 diabetes (45 on tirzepatide 15 mg, 44 on semaglutide 1 mg, 28 on placebo), 28 weeks. Tirzepatide ate −309.8 kcal less than placebo at lunch (P<0.001). Its extra −64.3 kcal against semaglutide wasn't significant (P=0.187).
- **Semaglutide trial (Friedrichsen 2021):** 35% lower lunch intake than placebo, with fewer cravings and better control of eating, over 20 weeks.
- **Brain-scan study (van Bloemendaal 2014):** 48 adults (lean, obesity, obesity plus type 2 diabetes). Exenatide lowered food-cue responses in the insula and amygdala in the groups with obesity.
- **Danish receipts study (Sørensen 2026, JAMA Network Open 9(1):e2555449):** 293 people who started a GLP-1 medicine against 884 matched non-users. Calories, sugar, carbohydrate and saturated fat per 100 g fell modestly, protein rose a little, and purchases moved away from ultra-processed food. GLP-1 receptor agonists are treated as one group.
- **SURMOUNT-4:** 783 started the lead-in and 670 were randomized (335 vs 335). The placebo group regained 14.0% and the group that stayed on tirzepatide lost a further 5.5%, weeks 36–88. Population matches: no diabetes.
- **Habit studies:** short sleep +385 kcal (Al Khatib 2017), ultra-processed diet about 500 kcal a day in 20 adults (Hall 2019, NIH), eating rate (Robinson 2014).
- **Animal and label sources:** Dickson 2012 (Gothenburg, injections into reward areas in rats), Gabery 2020, Adriaenssens 2019 and Hayashi 2023 all match how they're described. The label URL works.

**Framing:** labels for mice, rats and people are applied consistently. Observational data is called "linked, not proven", and cross-drug and population limits are stated.

**Safety:** the disclaimer, the prescriber line, the don't-stop line and an eating-disorder support line are all there. No dosing advice, and Dana is clearly labelled hypothetical.

What's left is minor: the title overstates the tirzepatide evidence slightly, one scope gap for Dana, and two on-screen labels that are missing a scope detail.

issues.claim: Tirzepatide Food Noise: Why Cravings Go Quiet
issues.problem: The title says as fact that tirzepatide quiets cravings. The tirzepatide trial measured appetite and lunch intake, not cravings. The craving data comes from semaglutide, and s43 says the trial doesn't measure food noise exactly. The video explains the 'why', but a softer verb would match the evidence better.
issues.fix: Tirzepatide and Food Noise: Why Cravings Can Go Quiet

issues.claim: For Dana, it's reassuring. The quiet she feels lines up with what trials measured, and it isn't just her trying harder.
issues.problem: The anchor trial enrolled only people with type 2 diabetes, and Dana's diabetes status isn't given. The line stretches the trial's scope a little.
issues.fix: For Dana, it's reassuring. The quiet she feels fits with what trials measured, even though that trial was in people with type 2 diabetes, and it isn't just her trying harder.

issues.claim: Extra daily intake after short sleep, meta-analysis
issues.problem: The muted-viewer test fails: the label doesn't say these were short-term experimental studies that restricted sleep. The narration's 'led people to eat' is fine for experimental data, but the card should carry the scope.
issues.fix: stat_label: "Extra daily intake after short sleep, short-term studies, meta-analysis"; narration: "In a meta-analysis of short-term sleep studies, cutting sleep led people to eat about three hundred and eighty-five extra calories a day."

issues.problem: The group sizes aren't tied to their arms, so a muted viewer can't tell which number belongs to which drug.

audio.soundNotes: Music sits well already (-13.5 dB under voice); pulled it down ~1.4 dB overall (0.85x) so pauses settle near -13 to -14 instead of -11.8, while staying inside the under-speech window. Trimmed a handful of cue spikes where SFX poked above the -14 dB speech ceiling (loudest offenders near -3 to -9 dB rel. voice around t≈28, 93, 139, 329, 376, 475.8, 563, 741.6, 756) so words stay fully legible; left the many quieter cues and the big pause/transition whooshes (already -6 to -12 dB) untouched. Added five bespoke atmosphere stingers for key beats (night open, food-noise reveal, blood-brain-barrier crossing, stress/sleep habit, and the closing "is the quiet real" hush) to add texture the stock kit can't give without adding clutter.

issues: Headline 'Your brain, calmer' is a bit generic/abstract but clear at phone size
Brain mascot may be slightly odd/unfamiliar as a 'character' but reads fine
Red circle on forehead is vague/unexplained, adds clutter without clear meaning
Generic emoji face doesn't connect visually to GLP-1/food topic
Less curiosity pull than the other two
'VS' plus two labels (CRAVINGS/BRAIN) is busier than 4-word limit implies, but still readable at phone size
Could be seen as slightly cute/mascot-heavy for a comparison format

thumbnail.reasoning: All three are legible at phone size with short, bold headlines and the brand mark small in the corner. #1 (reaction) is the weakest: the red circle on the emoji's head is ambiguous clutter, and the generic worried-emoji character doesn't visually connect to the video's food-noise/GLP-1 subject, giving it the least curiosity pull. #0 (before-after) matches the playbook's proven before-after pattern (brain mascot shifting from grey/stressed to pink/calm) and is clean and legible, but the payoff (contrast resolved instantly) slightly reduces the urge to click since the viewer already sees the 'answer'. #2 (versus) keeps the same instant-read clarity but adds a true two-sided conflict (craving donut vs. calm brain) with explicit labels, which creates a sharper emotional contrast and a bit more tension/curiosity ('who's louder now?') while staying fully honest to the video's content (food noise quieting). It reads in under a second even at 168px, uses only 4 words plus 2 short labels, and has the strongest single focal point plus emotional pull. Pick #2 as the best CTR candidate among those meeting the legibility bar.

issues.claim: Tirzepatide Food Noise: Why It Goes Quiet
issues.problem: The title presents food noise going quiet as certain for every user. The video gives a 'leading explanation' and lab appetite data from people with type 2 diabetes, and the description itself says 'why it can go quiet'. This is a wording-polish issue, not a misleading claim.
